Workspace Structure and Data Flow

This document traces the nested workspace structures in Powerful.jl from the top-level solver workspaces down to basic data structures, and explains the data flow through the gather-compute-scatter pattern.

Overview

Powerful.jl uses a layered architecture with clear separation of concerns:

  • State containers (DAE) hold the current solution and residuals
  • Computation workspaces orchestrate residual evaluation with zero allocation
  • Two solver paths (hand-baked Newton and NonlinearSolve.jl) share the same core infrastructure

Structure Hierarchy

Level 1: Solver Workspaces (User Interface)

Two alternative solver approaches, both pre-allocate all buffers for allocation-free iterations:

NewtonWorkspace (Hand-Baked Newton)

Location: src/solvers/powerflow.jl:806-828

NewtonWorkspace{SYS, JT, BT, PT}
├── cache::CachedAutodiffWorkspace{SYS}  # Residual evaluator
├── y::Vector{Float64}                    # Current solution iterate
├── g::Vector{Float64}                    # Current residuals
├── y_trial::Vector{Float64}              # Line search buffers
├── g_trial::Vector{Float64}
├── dy::Vector{Float64}                   # Newton update direction
├── J::JT                                 # Jacobian (Sparse/Dense)
├── jac_prep::PT                          # Prepared Jacobian (coloring)
├── jac_backend::BT                       # Differentiation backend
├── use_sparse::Bool
├── use_gpu::Bool
└── solver_fact::Base.RefValue{Any}       # Cached factorization (KLU/CUDSS)

Purpose: Orchestrates Newton-Raphson iterations for power flow solving. Holds iteration state and pre-allocated buffers for allocation-free solving.

Advantages:

  • Full control over Newton iteration
  • Supports GPU linear solve (CUDSS)
  • Transparent implementation
  • Explicit line search and damping

NonlinearSolveWorkspace (NonlinearSolve.jl Wrapper)

Location: src/solvers/powerflow.jl:209-218

NonlinearSolveWorkspace{SYS, JT, BT, PT}
├── cache::CachedAutodiffWorkspace{SYS}  # Residual evaluator (shared!)
├── prob::NonlinearProblem                # NonlinearSolve.jl problem
├── J::JT                                 # Jacobian matrix (Sparse/Dense)
├── jac_prep::PT                          # Prepared Jacobian (coloring)
├── jac_backend::BT                       # DifferentiationInterface backend
├── g_temp::Vector{Float64}               # Temp buffer for Jacobian eval
├── use_sparse::Bool
└── solver::Any                           # NonlinearSolve algorithm

Purpose: Pre-allocated workspace for NonlinearSolve.jl-based solver. Separates one-time setup (sparsity detection, coloring, problem construction) from allocation-free solves.

Advantages:

  • Access to multiple solvers (TrustRegion, LevenbergMarquardt, etc.)
  • Automatic line search and globalization
  • More robust for difficult cases
  • Battle-tested library

Convergence Point

Both solver workspaces contain the same CachedAutodiffWorkspace, meaning they share all residual evaluation infrastructure:

NewtonWorkspace                    NonlinearSolveWorkspace
       │                                    │
       │                                    │
       ├─── cache (CachedAutodiffWorkspace) ◄── Shared Infrastructure!
       │                                    │
       └────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                        ↓
            CachedAutodiffWorkspace
                        ↓
          SystemResidualWorkspace
                        ↓
           ResidualWorkspace (per model)
                        ↓
                      DAE

Level 2: CachedAutodiffWorkspace (Autodiff Cache Layer)

Location: src/analysis/autodiff_cache.jl:60-73

CachedAutodiffWorkspace{SYS}
├── sys::SYS                              # SystemModel reference
├── float_ws::SystemResidualWorkspace{Float64}
├── sys.dae::DAE{Vector{Float64}}
└── dual_cache::Dict{DataType, Tuple{Any, Any}}  # Cached Dual workspaces

Purpose: Avoids reallocating workspaces when ForwardDiff uses different Dual number configurations. Caches workspaces per Dual type for ~18% speedup in iterative solvers.

Key behavior: Callable as a function cache(g, y) - automatically dispatches to Float64 or Dual path based on input type:

function (cache::CachedAutodiffWorkspace)(g::AbstractVector, y::AbstractVector)
    if eltype(g) == Float64
        # Fast path: use pre-allocated Float64 workspace
        copyto!(cache.sys.dae.y, y)
        evaluate_system_residuals!(cache.float_ws, cache.sys.dae)
        copyto!(g, cache.sys.dae.g)
    else
        # Dual path: use cached Dual workspace
        ws_dual, dae_dual = cache.dual_cache[T]
        copyto!(dae_dual.y, y)
        evaluate_system_residuals!(ws_dual, dae_dual)
        copyto!(g, dae_dual.g)
    end
end

Level 3: SystemResidualWorkspace (System-Level Coordinator)

Location: src/system/system.jl:449-455

SystemResidualWorkspace{T, WS, Models, Metadata, ExtParams}
├── model_workspaces::NamedTuple{
│   ├── Bus => ResidualWorkspace{...}
│   ├── PQ => ResidualWorkspace{...}
│   ├── PV => ResidualWorkspace{...}
│   ├── Branch => ResidualWorkspace{...}
│   └── ...
│   }
├── model_vectors::NamedTuple{...}        # Cached model data
├── model_metadata::NamedTuple{...}       # Cached metadata
├── model_external::NamedTuple{...}       # External parameters
└── array_type::Type{<:AbstractVector}    # Vector or CuVector

Purpose: Coordinates residual evaluation across all model types. Contains one ResidualWorkspace per model type.

Responsibilities:

  • Owns all intermediate buffers (varvals, resvals per model)
  • Knows the system structure (which models exist, their dependencies)
  • Coordinates computation (gather → compute → scatter)
  • Manages memory locality (local buffers for cache efficiency)
  • Enables zero-allocation hot path

Level 4: ResidualWorkspace (Model-Level Computation)

Location: src/dae/residual_workspace.jl:151-164

ResidualWorkspace{T, AT, MaskT, VarAddrs, VarVals, ResAddrs, ResVals}
├── var_addrs::NamedTuple{                # Variable addresses (CPU)
│   ├── v => Vector{UInt64}
│   ├── theta => Vector{UInt64}
│   └── ...
│   }
├── var_vals::NamedTuple{                 # Variable values (CPU/GPU)
│   ├── v => AT (Vector or CuVector)
│   ├── theta => AT
│   └── ...
│   }
├── res_addrs::NamedTuple{                # Residual addresses (CPU)
│   ├── p => Vector{UInt64}
│   ├── q => Vector{UInt64}
│   └── ...
│   }
├── res_vals::NamedTuple{                 # Residual values (CPU/GPU)
│   ├── p => AT
│   ├── q => AT
│   └── ...
│   }
├── active_mask::MaskT                    # Bool mask (CPU/GPU)
└── n_instances::Int

Purpose: Pre-allocated workspace for a single model type's residual calculation. Uses NamedTuples for type-stable, dictionary-like access with zero runtime overhead.

Design Pattern: Enables the gather-compute-scatter pattern:

  • var_addrs + var_vals: Local copies of variables from DAE
  • res_addrs + res_vals: Local residual calculations before scattering to DAE
  • active_mask: Branchless masking for SIMD/GPU efficiency

Level 5: DAE (Global Equation System)

Location: src/dae/dae.jl:36-40

DAE{AT<:AbstractVector}
├── m::Int                                # Number of algebraic variables
├── y::AT                                 # Algebraic variables (CPU/GPU)
└── g::AT                                 # Algebraic residuals (CPU/GPU)

Purpose: Represents the system of differential-algebraic equations. Contains global variable and residual vectors.

Responsibilities:

  • Owns the global solution vector (y) and residual vector (g)
  • Defines the problem size (m variables, m equations)
  • Provides initialization (from Bus vm/va data)
  • Backend-agnostic (CPU or GPU via type parameter)
  • Minimal interface - just data, no computation logic

Future expansion: Will add differential variables (x, f) for dynamic simulation.

Level 6: Basic Data Structures

Addresses: Vector{UInt64} - indices into global DAE vectors Values: Vector{T} or CuVector{T} - actual numerical data NamedTuples: Type-stable containers with compile-time field access

Data Flow: Gather-Compute-Scatter Pattern

The system uses a gather-compute-scatter pattern for residual evaluation to achieve:

  • Zero allocation (all buffers pre-allocated)
  • Cache efficiency (local contiguous buffers)
  • SIMD/GPU optimization (vectorized kernels)

Hot Path: evaluatesystemresiduals!

Location: src/system/system.jl:601-625

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Zero global residuals: fill!(dae.g, 0)                      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ↓
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ For each model (Bus, PQ, PV, Branch...) │
        └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ↓
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ GATHER: Copy variables from global DAE to local │
    │   gather_variables!(ws, dae)                     │
    │   ws.var_vals.v[i] = dae.y[ws.var_addrs.v[i]]   │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ↓
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ COMPUTE: Model-specific residual calculation     │
    │   calc_residuals!(ws, model_vec, external)       │
    │   Dispatches to model kernel (PQ, PV, etc.)      │
    │   Uses ws.var_vals → computes ws.res_vals        │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ↓
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ SCATTER: Accumulate residuals to global DAE      │
    │   scatter_residuals!(ws, dae, metadata)          │
    │   Pass 1: PrivateRes & SharedRes(:add) - accum   │
    │   Pass 2: SharedRes(:set) - overwrite controls   │
    │   dae.g[ws.res_addrs.p[i]] += ws.res_vals.p[i]  │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ↓
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │          Next model...                  │
        └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              ↓
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 2. Synchronize (GPU only): CUDA.synchronize()                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Gather Operation

Location: src/dae/gather_scatter.jl:30-54

Copies variables from global DAE vector to local workspace buffers using indirect addressing:

# CPU: SIMD vectorized
@inline function gather_cpu!(dest, src, indices)
    @inbounds @simd for i in eachindex(indices)
        dest[i] = src[indices[i]]
    end
end

# GPU: CUDA kernel
function gather_kernel!(dest, src, indices, n)
    i = threadIdx().x + (blockIdx().x - 1) * blockDim().x
    if i <= n
        @inbounds dest[i] = src[indices[i]]
    end
    return nothing
end

Why gather?

  • Creates contiguous local copies (better cache performance)
  • Enables SIMD (no indirect indexing during compute)
  • Facilitates GPU coalesced memory access

Compute: Model-Specific Kernels

Each model implements calc_residuals! using the standardized kernel pattern:

# CPU kernel - pure math with @simd
@inline function pq_residual_kernel!(
    outputs::NamedTuple, params::NamedTuple, vars::NamedTuple,
    active::AbstractVector{Bool}, ::Type{<:Vector}
)
    @inbounds @simd for i in eachindex(outputs.p)
        mask = active[i]
        # Branchless masking: active → computed value, inactive → 0
        outputs.p[i] = mask * compute_p_residual(params, vars, i)
        outputs.q[i] = mask * compute_q_residual(params, vars, i)
    end
    nothing
end

# GPU kernel (device function + launcher)
function pq_residual_cuda_kernel!(outputs_p, outputs_q, params..., vars..., active, n)
    i = threadIdx().x + (blockIdx().x - 1) * blockDim().x
    if i <= n
        mask = active[i] ? one(...) : zero(...)
        @inbounds outputs_p[i] = mask * compute_p_residual(...)
        @inbounds outputs_q[i] = mask * compute_q_residual(...)
    end
    return nothing
end

Key principles:

  • Kernel = pure math only (no workspace access)
  • Branchless masking for SIMD/GPU efficiency
  • Type dispatch via AT parameter (Vector vs CuArray)

See residualcalculationdesign.md for detailed kernel patterns.

Scatter Operation: Two-Pass Algorithm

Location: src/dae/residual_workspace.jl:348-392

Accumulates residuals from local workspace to global DAE vector using a two-pass algorithm:

Pass 1: Accumulation (PrivateRes, SharedRes(:add))

for res in metadata.residuals
    # Skip setter SharedRes in first pass
    if res.access isa SharedRes && res.access.mode === :set
        continue
    end

    if mode === :private
        # Direct write for private residuals (e.g., branch flow limits)
        @inbounds @simd for i in eachindex(indices)
            if active[i]
                dae.g[indices[i]] = vals[i]
            end
        end
    else  # mode === :add
        # Accumulate for shared residuals (e.g., bus power balance)
        @inbounds for i in eachindex(indices)
            if active[i]
                dae.g[indices[i]] += vals[i]  # Multiple models contribute
            end
        end
    end
end

Pass 2: Setters (SharedRes(:set))

for res in metadata.residuals
    # Only process setter SharedRes
    if res.access isa SharedRes && res.access.mode === :set
        # Overwrites accumulated values (control equations like PV voltage control)
        @inbounds @simd for i in eachindex(indices)
            if active[i]
                dae.g[indices[i]] = vals[i]
            end
        end
    end
end

Why two-pass?

  • Pass 1: Multiple models contribute to bus power balance (PQ loads, PV generators, branches all add to bus equations)
  • Pass 2: Control equations (e.g., PV voltage setpoint) overwrite accumulated values

Example:

Bus power balance residual (Pass 1 accumulation):
  dae.g[bus_1_p] = 0
  dae.g[bus_1_p] += pq_load.p[0]      # +50 MW consumption
  dae.g[bus_1_p] += pv_gen.p[0]       # -100 MW generation
  dae.g[bus_1_p] += branch.p_i[0]     # +20 MW flowing out
  → dae.g[bus_1_p] = -30 MW (net injection)

PV voltage control (Pass 2 overwrite):
  dae.g[bus_2_q] = -30 MVAR          # From Pass 1
  dae.g[bus_2_q] = v - v_setpoint    # Overwrite with control equation
  → dae.g[bus_2_q] = 1.02 - 1.00 = 0.02 pu

Design Rationale: DAE vs SystemResidualWorkspace

Separation of Concerns

The architecture separates state (DAE) from operations (SystemResidualWorkspace):

DAE: State Container (Data)

Goal: Represent the mathematical structure and current state of the equation system.

Responsibilities:

  • Owns the global solution vector (y) and residual vector (g)
  • Defines the problem size (m variables, m equations)
  • Provides initialization (from Bus vm/va data)
  • Backend-agnostic (CPU or GPU via type parameter)
  • Minimal interface - just data, no computation logic

Analogy: Like a state object in React or a DataFrame in pandas - it's the data, not the operations.

SystemResidualWorkspace: Computation Engine (Operations)

Goal: Orchestrate residual computation across all model types with zero allocation.

Responsibilities:

  • Owns all intermediate buffers (varvals, resvals per model)
  • Knows the system structure (which models exist, their dependencies)
  • Coordinates computation (gather → compute → scatter)
  • Manages memory locality (local buffers for cache efficiency)
  • Enables zero-allocation hot path

Analogy: Like a QueryEngine in a database or Renderer in graphics - it's the operations that transform data.

Why This Separation Is Good

  1. Single Responsibility Principle: Each structure has one clear job
  2. Separation of Data and Computation: Classic functional programming principle
  3. Multiple Workspaces, One DAE: Different workspaces can operate on the same DAE
  4. Clean Interface for Solvers: Solvers only see the state (DAE), not implementation details
  5. Autodiff-Friendly: DAE is just arrays - ForwardDiff can handle it naturally

Tradeoffs

Memory Duplication

The workspace holds local copies of variables:

DAE.y (global)  →  [gather]  →  ResidualWorkspace.var_vals (local)
                                        ↓
                                   [compute]
                                        ↓
ResidualWorkspace.res_vals (local)  →  [scatter]  →  DAE.g (global)

Pro: Better cache locality, SIMD-friendly, enables GPU Con: 2x memory (local + global copies) Verdict: Good tradeoff - local buffers enable contiguous access, SIMD, and GPU efficiency

Complexity

The system has many layers, but each has a clear purpose.

Pro: Each layer has a clear, testable responsibility Con: Steeper learning curve, more indirection Verdict: Acceptable complexity for a research/production power systems simulator

Key Design Principles

  1. Zero Allocation: All buffers pre-allocated during workspace construction. Hot path (evaluate_system_residuals!) allocates zero memory after warmup.

  2. Type Stability: NamedTuples provide compile-time type information, allowing aggressive inlining and optimization.

  3. CPU/GPU Transparency: Same code structure for both backends. Array type (Vector vs CuVector) determines dispatch.

  4. Separation of Concerns:

    • NewtonWorkspace / NonlinearSolveWorkspace: Iteration mechanics
    • CachedAutodiffWorkspace: Autodiff caching
    • SystemResidualWorkspace: Model coordination
    • ResidualWorkspace: Single-model computation
    • DAE: Global state

  5. Branchless Masking: Inactive instances handled via multiplication by mask instead of conditional branches (SIMD/GPU friendly).

  6. Two-Pass Scatter: Ensures control equations (setters) correctly overwrite accumulated values from power balance equations.

Shared Infrastructure Benefits

Both Newton and NonlinearSolve paths share the same core infrastructure at CachedAutodiffWorkspace, enabling:

  • Code Reuse: Expensive residual evaluation infrastructure shared
  • Flexibility: Users choose robustness (NonlinearSolve) or performance (hand-baked Newton with GPU)
  • Maintainability: Model-specific code (calc_residuals!) written only once
  • Performance: Both achieve zero-allocation hot paths
  • Future-Proof: Easy to add new solver algorithms (just wrap CachedAutodiffWorkspace)

Performance Characteristics

Setup Phase (One-Time, Expensive)

  • Allocate all workspaces: ~1-10ms (depends on system size)
  • Compute sparsity pattern: ~10-100ms (structural analysis)
  • Jacobian coloring: ~10-50ms (greedy algorithm)
  • Total setup: ~50-200ms for large systems

Iteration Phase (Hot Path, Zero Allocation)

  • Residual evaluation: ~1-10ms (depends on system size, GPU vs CPU)
  • Jacobian computation: ~10-100ms (sparse colored ForwardDiff)
  • Linear solve: ~5-50ms (KLU on CPU, CUDSS on GPU)
  • Total iteration: ~20-150ms for large systems

Memory Usage

  • DAE vectors: 2 × m × sizeof(Float64) = ~16m bytes
  • Workspace buffers: ~4 × m × sizeof(Float64) = ~32m bytes (local copies)
  • Jacobian: nnz × sizeof(Float64) ≈ 5-10 × m bytes (sparse)
  • Total: ~50-60 bytes per variable

Example for IEEE 70k bus system (m ≈ 140,000):

  • DAE: ~2.2 MB
  • Workspaces: ~4.4 MB
  • Jacobian: ~14 MB
  • Total: ~20 MB
